nodes.label: Recovery window
nodes.sub:
how long after a mistake can a
conversation still be fixed?
nodes.desc: The number of turns between a model's first wrong answer and the point where giving it the missing information no longer fixes the answer. This is what my study measures.

nodes.label: Conversations degrade
nodes.desc: Accuracy drops when the same task is spread across several turns instead of asked all at once.

papers.sum: Across more than 200,000 simulated conversations, models did 39% worse on average when a task was split over several turns.
Shows that pressure from a user over several turns can make a model's answers less reliable.
Tests language models in more realistic conversations than standard benchmarks use.

nodes.label: When failure happens
nodes.desc: Studies that model when a model first fails, using survival analysis and Markov models.

papers.sum: Uses survival analysis to model how many turns pass before a model first becomes inconsistent.
Uses survival analysis to track how a model's safety wears down under repeated attacks.
Models an AI agent's reliability over many steps as a Markov chain.
Uses a hidden Markov model to describe how a model's reliability depends on what happened earlier in the interaction.

nodes.label: Can models recover?
nodes.desc: Models rarely fix their own mistakes, and outside help only partly restores accuracy.

papers.sum: Finds that planting errors in a model's reasoning doesn't get it to correct itself.
Finds signs that a model internally registers its mistakes, but that signal doesn't make it fix them.
Proposes ReIn, a way to help a model recover from errors in a conversation by adding guidance to its reasoning.
Studies when fixing code through a conversation with a language model works, and why it fails.
Trains models with reinforcement learning so they lose less accuracy over a conversation, partly by rewarding them for holding back when unsure.

nodes.label:
The model's own
earlier answers
nodes.desc: A model may treat what it already said as settled, even when it was wrong.

papers.sum: Finds that a model's own earlier replies in a conversation affect the answers it gives later.
Finds that whether a model flags an error depends on whether the text is labeled as its own.
Finds that AI models checking work go easier on it when the work is their own.
In a four-model test, models showed little or no preference for their own writing when revising it.

nodes.label:
Instructions given
in pieces
nodes.desc: Details from early in a conversation can be lost or misread when a request arrives across several messages.

papers.sum: Argues that models get lost because they misread what the user wants when instructions arrive in pieces.
Studies how models handle a conversation that switches context partway through.

nodes.label: User pushback
nodes.desc: When a user challenges an answer, a model may drop a correct answer or dig in on a wrong one.

papers.sum: Shows that pressure from a user over several turns can make a model's answers less reliable.
Introduces SYCON, a benchmark for measuring how often models give in to users over a multi-turn conversation.
Shows that different models react to being questioned or corrected in inconsistent ways.
Argues that some of what looks like caving to the user is a model changing its answer because it's uncertain.
Finds that a model's stated confidence follows how committed it is to an answer more than whether the answer is right.

nodes.label: The research plan
nodes.desc: How I'm measuring the recovery window: tasks whose answers are checked by code, and a repair probe at every turn after the first error.

nodes.label: Measurement cautions
nodes.desc: Problems to design around when measuring how models behave.

papers.sum: Shows that small numerical differences in how a model is run can change its outputs, even with the same settings.
Raises problems with using AI judges to score conversations.
